_about: Bible stories retold for children in three reading levels (4-6, 7-9, 10-12). Written for this app; each story points to the passage it retells.

stories.title: God Makes the World

text.4-6: In the very beginning there was nothing. Then God spoke, and light shone! God made the sky and the sea. He made the land, with trees and flowers. He made the sun, the moon and the stars. He made fish and birds and animals. Last of all, God made people, to be his children. God looked at everything and said, 'It is very good!' On the seventh day God rested.
text.7-9: Long ago, before anything else, there was God. God said, 'Let there be light,' and there was light! Day by day, God made the world. He made the sky, the oceans and the dry land. He made plants and trees, the sun, moon and stars, fish, birds and animals. On the sixth day God made people, a man and a woman, to look after the world and to know and love him. Everything God made was good, and people were very good. On the seventh day God rested and made the day special.
text.10-12: The Bible begins with God, who was there before everything. By his word alone he brings order out of emptiness: light, sky, sea and land, then plants, the sun, moon and stars, then creatures of the water, air and earth. Each time, God sees that it is good. People are the last and most special part: made 'in the image of God', able to know and love him, and trusted to take care of creation. God rests on the seventh day, which is why Sunday, the Lord's day, is a day for rest and for worship. The story is not a science lesson. It tells us who made us and why: because God is good, and the world is a gift.

talk: What is your favourite thing God made?
What does it mean to take care of what God made?
Why do you think God rested on the seventh day?

stories.title: Adam, Eve and the Garden

text.4-6: God made a beautiful garden, and put Adam and Eve in it. They had everything they needed. God said, 'You may eat from every tree, except one.' But a sly snake said, 'Eat it! God is not telling you the truth.' Eve and Adam ate the fruit. They broke God's rule, and they felt afraid. They hid from God. God was sad, but he still loved them. He promised that one day someone would come to put things right.
text.7-9: God made a garden called Eden for the first man and woman, Adam and Eve. They walked and talked with God, and had everything they needed. God gave them one rule: do not eat the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden. A sly serpent tricked Eve, saying that God was keeping something good from them. Eve ate the fruit and gave some to Adam. At once they felt ashamed and hid. God called, 'Where are you?' They had to leave the garden. But God did not stop loving them. He promised that someone from Eve's family would one day defeat the serpent. That someone is Jesus.
text.10-12: In the garden of Eden, Adam and Eve lived close to God. God gave one boundary: they must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The serpent whispered a lie, that God could not be trusted and that they could become like God. They chose to disobey, and the first thing sin did was break trust: they hid, blamed each other and were sent out of the garden. We call this the Fall. But notice that God goes looking for them ('Where are you?') and makes them clothes. He also promises that the woman's offspring will crush the serpent's head. The Church has always seen in this first promise the hint of Jesus and of Mary, the new Eve.

talk: Why did Adam and Eve hide?
When have you done something wrong and wanted to hide? What helped?
How did God show he still loved them?

stories.title: Cain and Abel

text.4-6: Adam and Eve had two sons, Cain and Abel. Abel looked after sheep. Cain grew food. Both brought gifts to God. God was pleased with Abel's gift, and Cain felt angry and jealous. God said, 'Be careful, Cain. Do what is good.' But Cain did not listen. He hurt his brother. This made God very sad. We must never be jealous or hurt others. We should be kind.
text.7-9: Cain and Abel were Adam and Eve's sons. Cain was a farmer and Abel was a shepherd. Each brought God an offering. God was pleased with Abel's gift, which came from the best he had. Cain grew angry and jealous. God warned him, 'Sin is waiting at your door, but you can master it.' Cain did not listen. He led Abel into a field and killed him. When God asked, 'Where is your brother?' Cain answered, 'Am I my brother's keeper?' The answer is yes: we are all meant to look after each other. Cain had to leave his home, but God still marked him with protection.
text.10-12: This is the first story of sin spreading from a heart to a family. Abel offers the best of his flock; Cain's offering is received with less favour, and jealousy grows into anger. God speaks to Cain before it is too late, saying sin is crouching at the door but he can rule over it. Cain chooses violence anyway, and then lies: 'Am I my brother's keeper?' God hears Abel's blood crying out from the ground. Even now God protects Cain from revenge, showing that mercy is stronger than vengeance. The Church remembers Abel as the first just man, and the Letter to the Hebrews says his faith still speaks.

talk: Why was Cain jealous?
What could Cain have done instead?
How can we be our brother’s or sister’s keeper today?

stories.title: Noah and the Ark

text.4-6: People stopped listening to God. But Noah loved God and did what was right. God said, 'Noah, build a big boat called an ark.' Noah built it. Then he took in his family and two of each kind of animal. Rain fell for many days. The ark floated safely. When the water went down, Noah sent out a dove. It came back with an olive leaf. God put a rainbow in the sky. It is a sign of his promise.
text.7-9: God saw that the world had filled with violence and sadness. But Noah was a good man who walked with God. God told him to build a great ark, a huge boat, and to bring his family and pairs of every animal inside. Noah trusted God and did exactly as he was told, even when others laughed. Then it rained and rained, and water covered the earth. The ark floated for many months. At last the water went down, and Noah sent out a dove. It came back with an olive leaf. When they stepped onto dry land, God promised never to flood the whole earth again and set his rainbow in the clouds.
text.10-12: Noah's story shows how serious God is about goodness, and how patient he is with people who trust him. Noah builds the ark for years on the word of God alone, which is what faith looks like: doing what God asks even when you cannot see the end. The flood is a kind of new beginning for creation, and the dove and olive branch have become signs of peace. God's covenant after the flood is with every living creature, with the rainbow as its sign. The Fathers of the Church saw the ark as a picture of the Church, carrying people safely through the waters, and Saint Peter links the flood to Baptism.

talk: How do you think Noah felt when people laughed?
What does the rainbow remind us of?
What is something God has asked you to trust him about?

stories.title: The Tower of Babel

text.4-6: Long ago everyone spoke the same language. They said, 'Let us build a tall tower to reach the sky. We will make ourselves famous!' But they forgot about God. God saw their proud hearts. He gave them different languages. Now they could not understand each other. So they stopped building, and spread across the earth. We should not be proud. We should thank God for all we have.
text.7-9: In the early days everyone on earth spoke one language. They found a plain and said, 'Let us build a city and a tower that reaches the heavens, and make a name for ourselves.' They were proud, and wanted to be great without God. God came down to look. He mixed up their speech so they could not understand one another. The building stopped and people scattered over the earth. The city was called Babel, which sounds like the Hebrew word for 'mixed up'.
text.10-12: Babel shows pride at its most ambitious: a united humanity using its skill to 'make a name for ourselves' instead of honouring God. God is not threatened by a tower; he is protecting people from the harm that comes when pride has no limits. The confusion of languages scatters them. The story has a beautiful answer in the New Testament. At Pentecost the Holy Spirit comes and people from every nation hear the apostles in their own language. What pride divided, the Spirit brings together in the Church.

talk: Why did the people want to build the tower?
What happened at Pentecost that reminds us of Babel?
What is the difference between being proud and being thankful?

stories.title: God Calls Abraham

text.4-6: God spoke to a man named Abraham. 'Leave your home and go to a new land. I will bless you.' Abraham was old, but he trusted God and went. Later God took Abraham outside at night. 'Look at the stars,' God said. 'Can you count them? Your family will be that big!' Abraham believed God.
text.7-9: Abraham, who was called Abram at first, lived in a land far from the one God had in mind. One day God said, 'Leave your country and your family and go to the land I will show you. I will make you a great nation, and through you all families of the earth will be blessed.' Abraham did not know where he was going, but he packed up and went with his wife Sarah. Years later, with no children yet, God took him outside under the night sky and said, 'Count the stars, if you can. That is how many people will come from you.' Abraham believed God.
text.10-12: With Abraham God begins his plan to save the world through one family. The call is simple and hard: leave everything familiar and trust. Abraham is seventy-five and childless, yet God promises a land, countless descendants and a blessing that will reach every nation. 'Abram believed the Lord, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness.' Saint Paul points to this verse again and again: Abraham is the father of all who believe. Every time we trust God without seeing the whole road, we follow him.

talk: Would you have gone with Abraham? Why?
What do the stars remind us about God’s promises?
When is it hard to trust God?

stories.title: Abraham and Isaac on the Mountain

text.4-6: God gave Abraham and Sarah a baby boy named Isaac, and they were so happy! When Isaac grew, God wanted to see how much Abraham trusted him. Abraham and Isaac climbed a mountain together. Isaac asked, 'Where is the lamb?' Abraham said, 'God will provide.' Just in time, an angel called out, 'Stop!' God showed them a ram. God had taken care of everything.
text.7-9: Abraham and Sarah waited many years, and at last God gave them a son, Isaac. He was the answer to a promise. One day God tested Abraham's trust. He asked him to take Isaac up a mountain and offer him to God. Abraham obeyed, though his heart must have been heavy. Isaac carried the wood and asked, 'Where is the lamb?' Abraham said, 'God will provide.' Then, just as Abraham was ready, an angel of the Lord cried out, 'Do not harm the boy!' Abraham looked up and saw a ram caught in the bushes, and offered that instead. God never wanted Isaac to be hurt. He wanted Abraham to know that God can always be trusted.
text.10-12: This is one of the most challenging stories in the Bible, so it is good to read it slowly. God tests Abraham, and Abraham trusts that God is faithful to his promise, even believing, as the Letter to the Hebrews says, that God could raise the dead. At the last moment God stops the sacrifice: he never asks for human sacrifice, and the story teaches that clearly. The ram is provided, 'God will provide.' Christians have long seen a picture of Jesus here: a beloved only son who carries the wood up a hill, and a Father who this time does not spare his Son but gives him for us. The place is called Moriah, later the Temple mount.

talk: What did Abraham mean when he said, “God will provide”?
Why do you think God stopped Abraham?
How is Isaac carrying the wood like Jesus carrying his cross?

stories.title: Jacob and Esau

text.4-6: Isaac and Rebekah had twin boys, Esau and Jacob. Esau was hairy and loved to hunt. Jacob stayed home. One day Esau was very hungry, and Jacob had some stew. Jacob tricked him, and later tricked their father too. This was not the right way to do things. Jacob had to run away. But God still loved Jacob, and did not give up on him.
text.7-9: Isaac and Rebekah had twin sons. Esau, the older, loved to hunt. Jacob was quiet and stayed by the tents. One day Esau came home very hungry and traded his rights as the oldest son for a bowl of Jacob's stew. Later, when old Isaac was nearly blind and ready to give his special blessing to Esau, Jacob dressed up and pretended to be his brother. Isaac blessed Jacob by mistake. Esau was furious, and Jacob had to flee. Jacob had done wrong, but God did not stop loving him. He would be the father of the twelve tribes of Israel.
text.10-12: God keeps choosing flawed people, and Jacob is a good example. His name means 'he grasps the heel', or 'he cheats', and he lives up to it: he trades a bowl of stew for his brother's birthright, then deceives his blind father to steal the blessing. The story does not call this right. Jacob pays a price in years of exile and in being tricked himself. Yet God's promise to Abraham and Isaac continues through him. It is a reminder that God's plan does not depend on how good we are, and that he gently works to change hearts, as he does with Jacob later at the river Jabbok.

talk: Was it right for Jacob to trick Esau and Isaac?
What happens when we try to get what we want by cheating?
How does God show mercy to Jacob?

stories.title: Jacob’s Ladder

text.4-6: Jacob was far from home, and he was alone. He put a stone under his head and fell asleep. In a dream he saw a ladder reaching up to heaven. Angels went up and down. God spoke: 'I am with you. I will never leave you.' Jacob woke up and said, 'God is here, and I did not know it!'
text.7-9: Jacob was running away from home, and night fell. He had no bed, so he used a stone for a pillow. In a dream he saw a ladder that reached from earth up to heaven, and God's angels were climbing up and down it. At the top stood the Lord, who said, 'I am with you and will watch over you wherever you go. I will bring you back.' Jacob woke up, amazed. 'Surely the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it!' In the morning he set up the stone as a marker and called the place Bethel, which means 'House of God'.
text.10-12: Jacob is alone, guilty and afraid, and it is exactly there that God meets him. The ladder joins heaven and earth, with angels carrying messages between them, and God repeats the promise made to Abraham and Isaac. He adds something Jacob needs most: 'I am with you.' Jacob calls it the gate of heaven. In John's Gospel Jesus tells Nathanael that he will see 'the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man': Jesus himself is the ladder, the meeting place of God and humanity. Every Catholic church is a Bethel, a house of God.

talk: Where have you felt that God was near, even when you did not expect it?
Why did Jacob call the place the gate of heaven?
How is Jesus like the ladder?

stories.title: Joseph and His Colourful Coat

text.4-6: Jacob loved his son Joseph very much. He gave Joseph a beautiful coat. Joseph's brothers were jealous. Joseph told them his dreams, and that made them more cross. One day, the brothers sold Joseph to travellers who took him to Egypt. Joseph was sad and far from home. But God was still with him.
text.7-9: Jacob had twelve sons, and he loved Joseph best, giving him a special coat of many colours. Joseph also had dreams in which his brothers bowed down to him, and when he told them, they grew angrier. One day, far from their father, the brothers seized Joseph, threw him into a pit and then sold him to traders going to Egypt. They dipped the coat in goat's blood and told their father Joseph was dead. Jacob was heartbroken. But God had not forgotten Joseph, and had a plan.
text.10-12: Joseph's story takes up the last part of Genesis, and it begins with family jealousy at its worst. Favouritism and Joseph's dreams stir up hatred, and the brothers sell their own brother as a slave for twenty pieces of silver. Notice how the story looks on the surface: a boy abandoned, a father deceived. But the Bible keeps whispering, 'The Lord was with Joseph.' What looks like the end is the first step in God's rescue of the whole family from famine. Joseph's rejection and rise has reminded many Christians of Jesus, also betrayed for silver by one of his own.

talk: Why were the brothers jealous?
How might Joseph have felt in the pit?
Can God use even bad things to bring about good?

stories.title: Joseph Forgives His Brothers

text.4-6: In Egypt, Joseph worked hard and God was with him. In time, he became a leader of Egypt. A great hunger came, and Joseph's brothers came to Egypt to ask for food. They did not know him! At last Joseph said, 'I am your brother Joseph!' The brothers were afraid. But Joseph said, 'I forgive you. God sent me here to save many people.' They hugged and cried.
text.7-9: In Egypt, Joseph was thrown into prison for something he did not do, but God was with him. He explained a dream for Pharaoh, which warned of seven good years and seven years of famine. Pharaoh made Joseph his chief helper, and Joseph stored up grain. When the famine came, Joseph's brothers travelled to Egypt to buy food. They bowed before him, not knowing who he was. At last Joseph cried out, 'I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?' The brothers were terrified. Joseph said, 'Do not be afraid. You meant to harm me, but God meant it for good.' He kissed them and wept, and the family was together again.
text.10-12: Years after being sold, Joseph has power to take revenge, but he chooses forgiveness. He tests his brothers gently, and sees they have changed: Judah offers himself in place of Benjamin. Then Joseph breaks down and reveals himself. His words, 'You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good,' do not excuse what the brothers did. They show a man who sees God's bigger plan and offers mercy. Joseph is a sign of Christ, who forgives even those who rejected him and who 'feeds' the whole world with the bread of life.

talk: How hard do you think it was for Joseph to forgive?
What changed in the brothers?
Who can you forgive this week?

stories.title: Baby Moses

text.4-6: In Egypt, the king was cruel to God's people, the Israelites. He wanted to hurt their baby boys. Moses' mother hid him as long as she could. Then she put him in a basket on the river. His sister Miriam watched. The king's daughter found him and loved him. She took him to be her son. Moses' own mother got to look after him too!
text.7-9: The people of Israel had grown in number in Egypt, and the new Pharaoh, afraid of them, made them slaves and ordered that every Hebrew baby boy be thrown into the Nile. A mother hid her baby for three months. When she could hide him no longer, she made a little basket of reeds, coated it with tar, and set it among the reeds by the river. Miriam, his sister, stood at a distance to see what would happen. Pharaoh's daughter came to bathe, found the basket and felt sorry for the crying baby. Miriam stepped forward: 'Shall I find a nurse for you?' So the baby's own mother was paid to care for him! The princess named him Moses, meaning 'drawn out'.
text.10-12: God's rescue of Israel begins with the courage of women: the midwives who refuse Pharaoh, a mother who risks everything and a sister who watches over a basket. The basket is like a small ark: the same word is used for Noah's boat. The child who will lead the people through the sea is first saved from water. God's plan is hidden in ordinary acts of love. Moses grows up in the palace but will always know where he comes from. Saint Stephen later praises how Moses was 'beautiful before God'.

talk: What was brave about what Moses’ mother and sister did?
How did God use Pharaoh’s own daughter?
When might God be working in a hidden way in your life?

stories.title: Moses and the Burning Bush

text.4-6: Moses looked after sheep in the desert. One day he saw a bush on fire, but it did not burn up! God called, 'Moses! Take off your shoes. This is holy ground.' God said, 'I have seen my people's pain. I will send you to help them.' Moses was scared. 'I will be with you,' said God.
text.7-9: Moses had left Egypt and become a shepherd. One day, on the mountain of Horeb, he saw a bush blazing with fire, but the bush did not burn up. As he stepped closer, a voice called, 'Moses, Moses! Take off your sandals, for this is holy ground.' It was God. 'I have seen the suffering of my people in Egypt, and I am sending you to bring them out.' Moses said, 'Who am I to do this?' and later, 'Who shall I say sent me?' God answered, 'I AM WHO I AM. Say, I AM has sent you.' God promised, 'I will be with you.'
text.10-12: In the desert God reveals his name. 'I AM WHO I AM' tells us God is the One who simply is, always present, not a god among many but the source of everything. He is also personal: he has seen, heard and come down to rescue. Moses makes every excuse: I am no one, they will not believe me, I cannot speak well. God answers each excuse with 'I will be with you.' The bush that burns without being consumed has been, for Christians, a picture of Mary, who carried God's fire without being harmed, and of God's presence that does not destroy but gives life.

talk: Why did God ask Moses to take off his sandals?
What excuses do we make when God asks something hard?
What does the name I AM tell us about God?

stories.title: The Passover and the Plagues

text.4-6: Moses asked the king, 'Let God's people go!' But the king said no. So God sent signs, to show his power. At last, God told the families to put lamb's blood on their doors and share a special meal. That night God passed over their homes and kept them safe. In the morning the king said, 'Go!' This is called the Passover.
text.7-9: Moses and his brother Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, 'The Lord says: Let my people go.' Pharaoh refused again and again, so God sent ten plagues on Egypt: the river turned to blood, then frogs, gnats and flies came, then more. Pharaoh's heart stayed hard. Before the last plague God told each Hebrew family to take a lamb without blemish, to mark their door frames with its blood and to eat a quick meal ready to travel. That night the angel of death passed over every marked door. Pharaoh finally let them go. Jews still keep Passover every year, and the Last Supper was a Passover meal.
text.10-12: The plagues are not just a contest of power. Each strikes at something the Egyptians worshipped, showing that the Lord alone is God. When Pharaoh still refuses, God tells Israel to take a spotless lamb and mark the doorposts with its blood, to eat the meal standing, ready to go. The blood protects them. This 'Passover' becomes Israel's yearly memorial of their freedom. For Christians, it points straight to Jesus, 'the Lamb of God', whose blood sets us free, and to the Eucharist, in which the new Passover is made present at every Mass.

talk: What did the lamb’s blood on the door mean?
Why do you think Pharaoh kept saying no?
How is the Mass like the Passover meal?

stories.title: Crossing the Red Sea

text.4-6: God's people left Egypt. But the king changed his mind and chased them! The people were at the sea, and they were afraid. Moses said, 'Do not be afraid. God will save you.' God made a path through the sea. The people walked across on dry ground! When the king's army followed, the water closed back. The people sang and danced to thank God.
text.7-9: The Israelites left Egypt, led by a tall cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night. But Pharaoh changed his mind and sent his army with chariots after them. The people were trapped between the army and the sea. They cried out in fear. Moses answered, 'Do not be afraid. Stand firm and watch the Lord rescue you today.' God told Moses to stretch out his staff. A strong wind blew all night and parted the sea, and the people walked through on dry land with walls of water on each side. When the Egyptians followed, the sea closed over them. Miriam took her tambourine and led the women in singing.
text.10-12: This is the great event of the Old Testament: God makes a way where there is no way. The people had been slaves, and they walk free through the waters, and the pursuing army is swept away. Miriam and Moses sing the first song of the Bible, praising God as their strength and salvation. The early Christians saw in the sea a picture of Baptism: we pass through the water from slavery to sin into the freedom of God's children. That is why the story of the Exodus is read at the Easter Vigil every year.

talk: How do you think the people felt standing at the sea?
Why did they sing?
What does the story teach us about trusting God when we feel trapped?

stories.title: Bread from Heaven

text.4-6: In the desert, the people were hungry. They grumbled. God heard, and said, 'I will send bread from the sky.' In the morning the ground was covered with a flaky white food called manna. Each person took just what they needed for the day. God gave them what they needed, every day.
text.7-9: A month after leaving Egypt, the people were in the desert, and their food ran out. They complained to Moses: 'In Egypt we had plenty of bread!' God said, 'I will rain bread from heaven for you.' Each morning, when the dew dried, there were fine flakes on the ground. The people said, 'What is it?' ('manna' in Hebrew). Moses told them, 'This is the bread the Lord has given you.' Each family gathered what they needed for the day, and no more. On the sixth day they gathered double, so they could rest on the Sabbath. For forty years God fed them.
text.10-12: The people are free, but they quickly forget the God who rescued them, and grumble. God does not scold them harshly; he feeds them. Manna teaches daily trust: gather only enough for today, and what is kept overnight spoils, except before the Sabbath. Jesus recalls the manna in John 6, after feeding five thousand: 'Your ancestors ate the manna and died; I am the living bread that came down from heaven.' This is why Catholics see manna as a sign of the Eucharist, and why we pray, 'Give us this day our daily bread.'

talk: What do you think manna tasted like?
Why could they only gather enough for one day?
How does Jesus give us bread from heaven?

stories.title: The Ten Commandments

text.4-6: God called Moses up Mount Sinai. God gave his people ten rules, called the Ten Commandments. They help us to love God and to love others. God said, 'Love me most of all. Honour your mother and father. Do not steal. Tell the truth.' God gave us these rules because he loves us and wants us to be happy.
text.7-9: Three months after leaving Egypt, the people came to Mount Sinai. The mountain shook with thunder and fire, and God spoke to Moses. 'I carried you out of Egypt on eagle's wings. Now, if you listen and keep my covenant, you will be my special people.' God gave the Ten Commandments: worship only me; do not misuse my name; keep the Sabbath; honour your father and mother; do not kill; be faithful in marriage; do not steal; do not lie; do not be greedy for what others have. They were written on two stone tablets. The first commandments are about loving God; the rest are about loving other people.
text.10-12: The commandments begin with a reminder: 'I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of slavery.' They are not a list of arbitrary rules but the way free people live in a covenant with the God who freed them. The first three tell us how to love God, and the other seven how to love our neighbour. Jesus summed them up: love God with all your heart, and your neighbour as yourself. The Catechism spends a large part of its teaching on them, because they show us what love looks like in daily choices.

talk: Which commandment is hardest for you? Why?
How do the commandments show love for God? For other people?
Why do you think God gave rules to people he had just set free?

stories.title: The Walls of Jericho

text.4-6: God's people came to a big city with high walls. God told Joshua, 'March around the city for six days. On the seventh day, shout!' The people did just what God said. They walked and walked. On the seventh day the priests blew the trumpets, the people shouted, and the walls fell down! God had kept his promise.
text.7-9: After Moses, Joshua led God's people into the promised land. The first city they met was Jericho, with huge walls and its gates shut tight. God gave Joshua a very odd plan: march around the city once a day for six days, with priests carrying the ark and blowing trumpets, and say nothing. On the seventh day they marched around seven times. Then the priests blew a long blast, the people gave a great shout, and the walls collapsed. The people walked in. God had given them the city, and he did it his way, so they would know the victory was his.
text.10-12: Jericho is about trusting God's way even when it seems strange. Joshua is not told to build siege engines. He is told to march, to carry the ark of God's presence and to listen. The story begins with an encounter: a commander of the Lord's army appears and says, 'Take off your sandals, the place where you stand is holy', echoing Moses at the bush. It also includes Rahab, who protected Israel's spies and was saved; she became an ancestor of Jesus. The story is also hard, since it involves war. The Church reads it carefully, remembering that the real victory is always God's mercy over sin.

talk: Why do you think God gave such an unusual plan?
What does Rahab teach us about trust?
What would it be like to walk and not say a word?

stories.title: Gideon and the Little Army

text.4-6: Gideon was afraid. But an angel said, 'God is with you, brave man.' God said, 'Your army is too big.' So Gideon had only three hundred soldiers. They had trumpets and jars with lights inside. At night they blew the trumpets and broke the jars. The enemy ran away! God showed that he is the one who saves.
text.7-9: Gideon was threshing wheat in secret because his people, the Israelites, were afraid of their enemies. An angel appeared and said, 'The Lord is with you, mighty warrior.' Gideon said, 'But I am the weakest in my family.' God said, 'I will be with you.' Thirty-two thousand men came to fight. God said, 'That is too many, or you will think you won by your own strength.' In the end only three hundred were left. At night they surrounded the enemy camp with trumpets and torches hidden in clay jars. They blew the trumpets and smashed the jars, and the enemy fled in panic.
text.10-12: Gideon starts out hiding and doubting, and God calls him ‘mighty warrior’ before he has done anything. The story turns on a surprising subtraction: the army shrinks from 32,000 to 300 so that no one can claim the victory as their own. The weapons are trumpets, torches and jars, signs of a battle that belongs to the Lord. Paul echoes this when he writes that God’s power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). Gideon is still imperfect; he asks for signs more than once. God is patient with him.

talk: Why did God make Gideon’s army smaller?
What makes you feel too small or too weak?
What does it mean to trust God’s power instead of our own?

stories.title: Ruth Stays Loyal

text.4-6: Ruth loved her mother-in-law Naomi. Naomi was sad and had to go home to Bethlehem. Ruth said, 'I will not leave you. Your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.' In Bethlehem Ruth picked up grain left in the field. A kind man named Boaz helped her. In time Ruth became part of King David's family.
text.7-9: A famine drove Naomi and her family from Bethlehem to the land of Moab. There her husband and sons died, leaving her with her daughters-in-law, Orpah and Ruth. Naomi decided to go back home and told them to stay with their own families. Orpah kissed her and went. But Ruth held on: 'Where you go I will go, where you live I will live. Your people will be my people and your God my God.' In Bethlehem, Ruth gathered leftover barley in the field of Boaz, a kind relative of Naomi. Boaz noticed her goodness and cared for her. In time they married, and their great-grandson was King David.
text.10-12: Ruth is a short book about 'hesed', loving loyalty. Ruth is a foreigner, a widow and poor, yet she chooses to bind herself to Naomi and to Naomi's God. The story shows God's quiet providence in ordinary events: a field, a harvest, a kind man. Boaz acts as 'redeemer', the relative who protects those in need, which is how Christians have understood Christ. And Ruth, from Moab, becomes the great-grandmother of David and so an ancestor of Jesus, named in Matthew's genealogy. God's family is wider than anyone expected.

talk: What did Ruth give up to stay with Naomi?
How did Boaz show kindness?
Who needs your loyalty and friendship?

stories.title: Hannah Prays for a Baby

text.4-6: Hannah wanted a baby more than anything. She went to the house of God and prayed and prayed. She cried, but she trusted God. God heard her. She had a little boy and named him Samuel. Hannah was so thankful. She brought Samuel to serve God, and she sang a song of thanks.
text.7-9: Hannah was sad because she had no children. Each year she went to the tent of worship at Shiloh. One year she prayed so hard, with tears, that Eli the priest thought something was wrong with her. 'I am pouring out my heart to the Lord,' she said. Eli told her to go in peace. God answered her prayer, and she had a son. She called him Samuel, which sounds like 'God has heard'. When Samuel was still small, Hannah kept her promise and took him to serve God at the tent of worship. She sang a song of joy: 'My heart rejoices in the Lord.'
text.10-12: Hannah’s story begins in longing and ends in a song. She does not hide her pain from God; she pours it out. Eli misunderstands her at first, and then blesses her, showing that prayer is sometimes a quiet thing that only God sees. After Samuel is born, Hannah gives him back to God, trusting that the gift is not lost but safe. Her song is a model for Mary’s Magnificat: both praise a God who lifts the lowly and fills the hungry. Catholics see in Hannah a picture of persevering prayer.

talk: What did Hannah do when she was sad?
Why do you think she gave Samuel back to God?
What would you tell God about today?

stories.title: God Calls Samuel

text.4-6: Samuel was a boy who helped in God's house. One night he heard a voice, 'Samuel!' He ran to Eli. 'Here I am. You called me.' Eli said, 'I did not call. Go back to bed.' This happened again. Then Eli said, 'It is God. Say, Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.' Samuel did, and God spoke to him.
text.7-9: Samuel lived and worked in the house of the Lord with the old priest Eli. In those days, God did not often speak to his people. One night, Samuel heard a voice call, 'Samuel!' He ran to Eli. 'Here I am; you called me.' 'I did not call,' said Eli. 'Go back and lie down.' It happened a second time, and a third. Then Eli understood that God was calling the boy. 'Go and lie down, and if he calls again, say, Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening.' Samuel did, and God gave him a message. Samuel grew up to be a great prophet, and all Israel knew the Lord was with him.
text.10-12: God chooses a child to hear his voice at a time when 'the word of the Lord was rare'. Samuel does not recognise God at first, and it takes the patience of old Eli to help him see. Three times God calls him by name: God knows each of us by name. The answer Eli teaches him, 'Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening', has become a prayer for many. The message to Samuel is hard (Eli's household will fall), and Samuel is afraid to tell it, but he tells the truth. Listening for God includes courage and honesty.

talk: Why did Samuel think it was Eli who called him?
How can we listen for God?
What prayer could you pray like Samuel?

stories.title: David and Goliath

text.4-6: A giant named Goliath scared the whole army. But young David was not afraid. 'God will help me,' he said. David picked up five smooth stones and his sling. He ran toward Goliath. He threw one stone, and Goliath fell down! God helped David win. David knew it was God's help, not his own strength.
text.7-9: The Philistine army had a champion, a giant named Goliath, over nine feet tall. Every day he shouted at Israel's army, and no one dared to fight him. David, a young shepherd, came to bring food to his brothers. He heard Goliath and said, 'Who is this man, to insult the armies of the living God?' King Saul gave David his armour, but it was too big. David took his shepherd's staff, five smooth stones and a sling. 'You come with a sword and spear,' he said to Goliath, 'but I come in the name of the Lord.' David slung a stone, and it struck Goliath, who fell down. The Philistines ran away.
text.10-12: Everyone expects strength to win, but this story shows trust in God defeating fear. David knows what to do because he has protected his flock from lions and bears, and he sees that he is not alone: 'The battle is the Lord's.' Saul's armour does not fit; David must fight as himself. The story is about courage, but also humility: David credits God, not himself. Many have seen in David a sign of Christ, the shepherd who faces the enemy for the sake of the people and wins what they cannot.

talk: Who or what is the “Goliath” you are afraid of?
Why did David refuse Saul’s armour?
What did David trust in?

stories.title: The Lord Is My Shepherd

text.4-6: David looked after sheep, and he knew what a good shepherd does. He wrote a song: 'The Lord is my shepherd. I have everything I need. He leads me beside quiet water. Even in a dark valley, I am not afraid, for you are with me.' God looks after us like a shepherd looks after his sheep.
text.7-9: Before David was king he was a shepherd, and he knew how a shepherd cares for his sheep: finding green grass and still water, guiding them on safe paths, and protecting them from wolves with his rod and staff. In Psalm 23, David says God is like that: 'The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want. Even in the darkest valley I will fear no evil, for you are with me.' God sets a table for us and fills our cup to overflowing. 'Goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life.' Jesus later said, 'I am the Good Shepherd.'
text.10-12: Psalm 23 is the most loved psalm in the world, and it is a good one to learn by heart. It begins with trust, 'I shall not want', and moves through quiet pastures, right paths and the valley of the shadow of death, where the psalm turns from 'he' to 'you': in the dark, God is not spoken about but spoken to. The rod and staff are for protecting the sheep. The banquet table and the overflowing cup have made Christians think of the Eucharist, and the 'house of the Lord' of heaven. Jesus applies this image to himself in John 10: the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep.

talk: What does a shepherd do for the sheep?
When have you felt God was with you in a dark valley?
What does it mean that goodness and mercy will follow us?

stories.title: Solomon Asks for Wisdom

text.4-6: Solomon became king when he was young. In a dream God said, 'Ask for anything you want.' Solomon did not ask for money or a long life. He said, 'Please give me a wise and listening heart.' God was very pleased. God gave him wisdom, and many good things besides.
text.7-9: When David died, his son Solomon became king. One night God appeared to him in a dream and said, 'Ask what I should give you.' Solomon said, 'I am only a young man, and I do not know how to rule. Give me a listening heart so that I can tell right from wrong.' God was pleased that he had not asked for riches or fame. 'I will give you a wise heart, and I will also give you what you did not ask for.' Soon after, two women came to Solomon, both claiming the same baby. Solomon said, 'Cut the baby in two.' One woman cried, 'No! Give her the baby!' Solomon knew she was the true mother.
text.10-12: Solomon's request is what the Bible calls 'a listening heart' (in Hebrew, one that hears). He knows his weakness and asks for what he needs to serve God's people, not for himself. The test of the two women shows wisdom as the ability to see the heart of a matter. Later Solomon builds the Temple in Jerusalem. The story is also a warning: Solomon's wisdom grows weak when he turns from God. Jesus says that 'something greater than Solomon is here'. The Church has always prayed for the gift of wisdom as one of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

talk: What would you have asked for?
How did Solomon know who the real mother was?
How can we ask God for wisdom?

stories.title: Elijah and the Quiet Voice

text.4-6: Elijah was a prophet who told people to follow God. God took care of him. Birds brought him bread and meat. Later Elijah felt scared and hid in a cave. There was a big wind, an earthquake and a fire. But God was not in those. Then there was a quiet, gentle whisper. God was there, speaking softly to Elijah.
text.7-9: Elijah was a prophet in a time when the king and queen worshipped a false god, Baal. Elijah told them there would be no rain until God said so. God told Elijah to hide by a stream, and ravens brought him bread and meat each morning and evening. Later, a poor widow shared the last of her flour and oil with him, and God made the jar never run out. At last, after a great showdown on Mount Carmel, Elijah ran away in fear and wanted to give up. God fed him through an angel, and Elijah walked forty days to Mount Horeb. There came a great wind, an earthquake and a fire, but the Lord was not in them. Then came a gentle whisper, and Elijah hid his face.
text.10-12: Elijah stands for the courage to tell the truth to power, but this story is about what happens afterwards: he is exhausted and afraid, and asks to die. God's response is gentle: sleep, bread and water, an angel's touch. On the mountain where Moses met God, Elijah expects the Lord in spectacular signs, and finds him in 'a sound of sheer silence'. It is a reminder to make room for silence in prayer. God also corrects Elijah's loneliness by telling him there are seven thousand faithful people and gives him Elisha as a companion. At the Transfiguration, Elijah appears with Moses beside Jesus.

talk: How did God take care of Elijah?
Where do you find quiet to listen for God?
Why was God not in the wind, earthquake or fire?

stories.title: Naaman and the River

text.4-6: Naaman was a great soldier, but he had a bad skin sickness. A little girl said, 'There is a prophet who can help you.' Naaman went to Elisha. Elisha said, 'Wash in the river Jordan seven times.' Naaman was cross. It seemed too easy! But he did it, and his skin became clean and new. Naaman thanked God.
text.7-9: Naaman was the commander of the army of Aram, and he had a serious skin disease. A young servant girl from Israel told his wife, 'There is a prophet in Samaria who could heal him.' Naaman traveled to Israel with horses, silver and gold. Elisha did not even come out to meet him. He sent a message: 'Go and wash seven times in the Jordan.' Naaman was angry. 'Our rivers are better!' he said. But his servants said, 'If he had asked you to do something hard, you would have done it. Why not try something simple?' Naaman washed, and his skin became like a child’s. He said, 'Now I know there is no God in all the earth except in Israel.'
text.10-12: Naaman is a powerful man, but he needs help, and the one who points the way is a nameless slave girl. He expects a grand cure with a show of power; God gives an ordinary river and a simple command. His pride nearly keeps him from it, until his servants speak up. Jesus later says that, in the days of Elisha, many Israelites had leprosy but only Naaman, a foreigner, was cured (Luke 4:27), showing that God’s healing is for everyone. The Fathers saw the seven washings and the Jordan as a sign of Baptism.

talk: Who helped Naaman, and why is that surprising?
Why did Naaman not want to wash in the Jordan at first?
When is it hard to do something simple that God asks?

stories.title: Jonah and the Big Fish

text.4-6: God said to Jonah, 'Go to the city of Nineveh and tell the people to stop doing wrong.' Jonah did not want to go. He hopped on a boat to go far away! A big storm came. Jonah was thrown into the sea, and a great fish swallowed him! Jonah prayed inside the fish for three days. God saved him. Jonah went to Nineveh. The people said sorry, and God forgave them.
text.7-9: God told Jonah to go to Nineveh, a great city, and warn the people to turn away from their evil. Jonah did not want to, because the people of Nineveh were enemies of Israel. He boarded a ship heading the opposite way. God sent a huge storm. The sailors were terrified, and Jonah said, 'Throw me into the sea, and it will become calm.' They did, and the sea went quiet. God sent a great fish that swallowed Jonah. For three days and nights Jonah prayed from inside the fish, and then the fish spat him onto dry land. This time Jonah went to Nineveh and preached, and everyone, even the king, said sorry. God forgave them. Jonah was cross about it, but God said, 'Should I not care about this great city?'
text.10-12: Jonah is a story with a surprising point. The prophet who runs from God is more stubborn than the sailors or the pagan city. The sailors turn to God; the Ninevites repent after one short sermon; only Jonah is angry that God is merciful. The book ends with God's question to him and to us: should I not pity them? Jesus points to the 'sign of Jonah': three days in the fish, and the Church sees in it a sign of his three days in the tomb and rising again. Mercy is meant to reach everyone, even our enemies.

talk: Why did Jonah run away?
Why was Jonah angry when God forgave Nineveh?
Who is hard for you to forgive or to care about?

stories.title: Daniel in the Lions’ Den

text.4-6: Daniel prayed to God three times every day. Some men made a law: nobody could pray to anyone except the king. But Daniel still prayed to God. The king had to put Daniel in a pit with lions. All night God sent an angel who closed the lions' mouths. In the morning Daniel was safe! The king said, 'Daniel's God is the living God!'
text.7-9: Daniel served under King Darius in Babylon and was so honest and wise that the king planned to put him in charge of the whole kingdom. Jealous officials tricked the king into signing a law: for thirty days, anyone who prayed to a god or man other than the king would be thrown into the lions' den. Daniel heard about the law, but he went home, opened his windows towards Jerusalem and prayed three times a day, as he always did. He was arrested, and the king, who liked Daniel, was very sad. 'May your God rescue you,' he said. At dawn, the king hurried to the den. 'Daniel! Has your God saved you?' 'My God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths,' Daniel called.
text.10-12: Daniel lives in exile, in the court of a foreign king, and he does not hide his faith. When a law forbids prayer, he does the simplest, bravest thing: he keeps praying, in the open, just as he did before. His faithfulness is not stubbornness; he does not lead a revolt or insult the king. The king himself ends the story by praising Daniel's God. Early Christians saw in Daniel a picture of martyrs, and in the sealed den a sign of Christ's tomb, from which he came out alive.

talk: Why did Daniel keep praying?
What could happen if we hide our faith?
What is your daily habit of prayer?

stories.title: Queen Esther

text.4-6: Esther became queen. A wicked man planned to hurt her people, the Jews. Her cousin Mordecai said, 'Maybe you are queen for a time like this.' Esther was afraid, but she prayed and was brave. She told the king. The king stopped the plan, and God's people were saved.
text.7-9: Esther was a Jewish girl who became queen of Persia, though no one knew she was Jewish. A wicked official, Haman, tricked the king into signing a law to destroy all the Jews. Her cousin Mordecai begged Esther to go to the king. It was dangerous, because anyone who came to the king without being called could be put to death. Esther asked her people to fast and pray for three days, and then said, 'If I perish, I perish.' She went in, and the king held out his sceptre to her. At two banquets she told him the truth. The king stopped Haman's plot, and the Jews were saved. The feast of Purim remembers it.
text.10-12: In Esther's story God's name is never mentioned, yet his hand is felt everywhere. A hidden queen, an unlikely moment and a few brave words change history. Mordecai's question, 'Who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?', is for every one of us. Esther does not act alone: she asks the community to pray and fast first. In the Catholic Bible Esther's own prayer is included, 'Lord, help me, who am alone and have no helper but you.' She is a model of courage that depends on God.

talk: What made Esther brave?
How did prayer and fasting help Esther?
What might God be asking you to do “for such a time as this”?

stories.title: Tobias and the Angel

text.4-6: Tobias had to go on a long trip. His father said, 'Find a guide to go with you.' A kind man named Azarias joined him. Azarias helped Tobias on the road. At the end, he said, 'I am the angel Raphael. God sent me to help you.' The angel Raphael means 'God heals'. God sends angels to look after us.
text.7-9: Old Tobit was blind and poor, though he had always been generous and good. He sent his son Tobias on a long journey to collect some money. Tobias's mother worried, so Tobias went with a guide, Azarias, and his little dog. On the way, a big fish leapt out of the river. Azarias told Tobias to keep the fish's heart, liver and gall, which would be useful as medicine. At the end of the journey, Tobias used the medicine to heal his father's eyes and to help a young woman named Sarah. Then Azarias said, 'I am Raphael, one of the seven angels who stand before God.' Raphael means 'God heals'.
text.10-12: The Book of Tobit is full of good humour and warmth, and it is only in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles. Tobit buries the dead and gives to the poor even when it costs him; young Sarah prays through her sorrow; and God hears both prayers, sending the angel Raphael, who walks with Tobias as a friend. Raphael is one of the three archangels the Church honours. The story reminds us that God cares about family, travel, courtship and the small journeys of life, and that angels are real helpers, though we usually do not recognise them until later.

talk: How did Raphael help Tobias without being noticed?
What does the name Raphael mean?
How do angels help us today? Do you pray to your guardian angel?

stories.title: The Angel Visits Mary

text.4-6: In a town called Nazareth lived a girl named Mary. One day the angel Gabriel came to her. 'Hello, Mary! God is with you. You will have a baby, and you will call him Jesus. He is the Son of God.' Mary said, 'I am the Lord's servant. Let it be as you say.' Mary trusted God.
text.7-9: Mary was a young woman in Nazareth, promised in marriage to Joseph. One day the angel Gabriel appeared and said, 'Greetings, favoured one! The Lord is with you.' Mary was surprised and wondered what this greeting meant. 'Do not be afraid, Mary. You will have a son and you will name him Jesus. He will be called the Son of the Most High, and his kingdom will never end.' Mary asked, 'How can this be?' The angel said the Holy Spirit would come upon her, 'for nothing is impossible with God.' Mary answered, 'I am the Lord's servant. May it be done to me as you say.' We say 'yes' like Mary in the prayer called the Angelus.
text.10-12: Everything in the New Testament begins with a question and a 'yes'. Gabriel greets Mary with a title no one else is given, 'full of grace' (or 'favoured one'). Mary is troubled but not frightened away; she asks an honest question, and is told that the Holy Spirit will overshadow her, as the cloud overshadowed the tent of meeting in the desert. She is free to say no, and she says 'Let it be done to me according to your word.' Catholics pray the Hail Mary, which begins with Gabriel's greeting, and the Angelus, which remembers this moment three times a day. The Church calls Mary the new Eve: where Eve's 'no' brought sin into the world, Mary's 'yes' opens the way for Christ.

talk: What did Mary say to the angel?
Why do you think Mary said yes?
How can you say yes to God today?

stories.title: Mary Visits Elizabeth

text.4-6: Mary hurried to visit her cousin Elizabeth, who was going to have a baby too. When Mary said hello, Elizabeth's baby jumped for joy! Elizabeth said, 'You are blessed, Mary!' Mary sang a happy song to God: 'My soul praises the Lord.' We call it the Magnificat.
text.7-9: After the angel's visit, Mary set off in a hurry to the hill country of Judea to see her older cousin Elizabeth, who was expecting a baby, John, after many years of waiting. As soon as Elizabeth heard Mary's greeting, the baby leapt in her womb and she was filled with the Holy Spirit. 'Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the child you carry!' she cried. 'Why am I so honoured that the mother of my Lord should come to me?' Mary responded with a song: 'My soul proclaims the greatness of the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Saviour.' She stayed with Elizabeth about three months, helping her.
text.10-12: Mary's first act after saying yes is to go in haste to help someone else. The meeting of two mothers is full of joy: John leaps in the womb, the first to recognise the Lord, and Elizabeth speaks the words that form the second half of the Hail Mary. Mary's song, the Magnificat, is sung at Evening Prayer every day by the Church. It echoes Hannah's song in the Old Testament and praises God who lifts up the lowly and fills the hungry with good things. She does not keep the credit for herself: 'He who is mighty has done great things for me.'

talk: Why did Mary hurry to Elizabeth?
What does Mary’s song say about God?
Who could you visit or help this week?

stories.title: Jesus Is Born

text.4-6: Mary and Joseph travelled to Bethlehem. There was no room at the inn. So Jesus was born in a stable, and Mary laid him in a manger. Out in the fields, angels sang to the shepherds, 'Good news! A Saviour is born!' The shepherds ran to see him. Jesus, God's own Son, was a tiny baby.
text.7-9: The emperor ordered a count of all the people, so Joseph took Mary, who was about to have her baby, to Bethlehem, the city of David. The town was crowded and there was no room for them in the inn. There in a stable, Mary gave birth to her son. She wrapped him in cloths and laid him in a manger, a feeding trough for animals. Out on the hills, shepherds were watching their sheep at night when an angel appeared. 'Do not be afraid. I bring you good news of great joy for all people. Today a Saviour has been born to you.' A host of angels sang, 'Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth!' The shepherds hurried to Bethlehem and found the baby, just as the angel said.
text.10-12: Luke tells the greatest event in history with quiet details: a census, a crowded town, a feeding trough. God enters the world as a poor baby, born outside the inn. The first people to hear are not kings or priests but shepherds, ordinary workers who were not highly regarded. 'Bethlehem' means 'house of bread', and Jesus is laid in a manger, a place where food is put, hinting at the Eucharist. Mary 'treasured all these things and pondered them in her heart.' The Church celebrates this at Christmas Mass, and the angels' song, 'Glory to God in the highest', is sung every Sunday.

talk: Why do you think God chose a stable and shepherds?
What did the angels say?
How can we make room for Jesus in our hearts?

stories.title: The Wise Men

text.4-6: Wise men saw a bright new star. They knew it meant a great king had been born. They followed it a long way. At last, they found Jesus with Mary. They knelt down and gave him presents: gold, frankincense and myrrh. Then they went home a different way. We celebrate this on a day called Epiphany.
text.7-9: Far to the east, wise men who studied the stars saw a new star rise and knew it meant a new king of the Jews had been born. They travelled to Jerusalem and asked King Herod where to find him. Herod was frightened and jealous, and asked them to come back and tell him. The star led them to Bethlehem, where it stopped over the house. They saw the child with Mary his mother, and they knelt and worshipped him. They gave him gold, frankincense and myrrh. God warned them in a dream not to go back to Herod, so they went home another way.
text.10-12: The Magi are the first people from outside Israel to worship Jesus, and we celebrate the feast of the Epiphany for them: the 'showing' of Christ to all nations. Their gifts have been seen as signs of who Jesus is: gold for a king, frankincense for God, and myrrh, used for burial, for the one who would die. Herod's fear is also real, and it leads to the flight to Egypt. The wise men show that God can be found by anyone who searches sincerely, and that finding him changes our road: they 'went home by another way'.

talk: What gift would you bring to Jesus?
Why did the wise men go home another way?
Who helps lead you to Jesus, like the star?

stories.title: Jesus in the Temple

text.4-6: When Jesus was twelve, he went with Mary and Joseph to Jerusalem. On the way home, they could not find him! They looked and looked. After three days, they found him in the Temple, talking with the teachers. Mary said, 'Why did you do this?' Jesus said, 'I must be in my Father's house.' Then he went home and obeyed his parents.
text.7-9: Every year Mary and Joseph went to Jerusalem for the feast of Passover. When Jesus was twelve, he went with them. On the way home, they travelled with a big group of relatives and friends, and only after a whole day did they realise Jesus was not with them. Worried, they went back to Jerusalem. After three days they found him in the Temple, sitting among the teachers, listening and asking questions. Everyone was amazed at his understanding. Mary said, 'Son, why have you done this to us? We have been looking for you anxiously.' Jesus answered, 'Why were you looking for me? Did you not know I must be in my Father's house?' Then he went home with them and was obedient.
text.10-12: This is the only story of Jesus' boyhood in the Gospels. It reveals two things at once: Jesus is truly God's Son, who knows the Temple is his Father's house, and he is truly a child who goes home with his parents and obeys them. Mary and Joseph do not fully understand, and Luke says that Mary 'treasured all these things in her heart'. The three days of searching foreshadow another three days of loss, after the cross. This is the fifth of the Joyful Mysteries of the Rosary, 'The Finding of the Child Jesus in the Temple'.

talk: Why did Mary and Joseph look so long?
What did Jesus say about his Father’s house?
How can we show we love God’s house, the church?

stories.title: Jesus Is Baptised

text.4-6: Jesus went to the Jordan River, where John was baptising people. John said, 'You should baptise me!' But Jesus said, 'This is how we do what God wants.' John baptised Jesus. Then the sky opened. The Holy Spirit came down like a dove, and God said, 'This is my beloved Son. I am very pleased with him.'
text.7-9: John the Baptist lived in the desert and told people to turn back to God and be baptised in the river Jordan as a sign of being sorry for their sins. One day Jesus came from Galilee to be baptised by John. John tried to stop him: 'I need to be baptised by you!' Jesus said, 'Let it be so now, for we must do all that God asks.' So John baptised him. As Jesus came up out of the water, the heavens opened and the Spirit of God came down on him like a dove, and a voice from heaven said, 'This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.' All three Persons of the Trinity are there: the Father speaks, the Son is baptised, and the Spirit comes as a dove.
text.10-12: Jesus has no sin, so why is he baptised? He goes down into the waters to stand with sinners and to make the water holy for us. At the Jordan, the heavens open, the Spirit descends and the Father speaks: the first full revelation of the Holy Trinity in the Gospels. The words 'beloved Son' echo Isaac, and 'with whom I am well pleased' echo the servant in Isaiah. In our own baptism, we too are named God's beloved children. Catholics trace the sign of the cross and make a little renewal of baptism with holy water each time we enter a church.

talk: Why did Jesus want to be baptised?
Who is in the story: Father, Son and Spirit?
What do you remember about your own baptism?

stories.title: Jesus Calls His Friends

text.4-6: Some men were fishing by the lake. They had caught nothing all night! Jesus said, 'Throw your nets again.' Simon did, and the nets filled with so many fish they began to tear! Jesus said, 'Follow me. I will make you fishers of people.' They left their boats and followed Jesus.
text.7-9: Simon, Andrew, James and John were fishermen on the Sea of Galilee. After a long night of fishing, they had caught nothing. Jesus was teaching a crowd on the shore and asked to use Simon's boat. When he finished, he said, 'Go out into deep water and let down your nets.' Simon said, 'Master, we worked hard all night and caught nothing, but because you say so, I will.' The nets became so full of fish that they began to tear, and other boats had to come to help. Simon fell at Jesus' knees: 'Go away from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man!' Jesus said, 'Do not be afraid. From now on you will be catching people.' They pulled their boats up on the shore, left everything and followed him.
text.10-12: Jesus chooses ordinary people: fishermen, a tax collector, a zealot. He does not wait until they are perfect. Peter's reaction is the right one: faced with Jesus' power and goodness, he knows his own weakness. Jesus does not leave him there; he says, 'Do not be afraid', and gives him a new mission. The Church describes the first apostles as the foundation of the Church, and Peter's boat has been a picture of the Church ever since. The Lord still calls all of us, in different ways, to follow him.

talk: Why did the nets break?
What did Peter say, and what did Jesus say to him?
What might it mean to “leave your nets”?

stories.title: Water into Wine

text.4-6: Jesus and his friends went to a wedding. The wine ran out! Mary said to the servants, 'Do whatever he tells you.' Jesus asked them to fill big jars with water. Then he turned the water into the best wine! It was Jesus' first miracle. Mary helped, and the servants did as they were asked.
text.7-9: In the village of Cana in Galilee, there was a wedding feast, and Jesus, his mother Mary and his disciples were invited. Part way through, the wine ran out, which would have embarrassed the family. Mary quietly told Jesus, 'They have no wine.' Jesus said, 'My hour has not yet come.' But Mary turned to the servants and said, 'Do whatever he tells you.' Jesus asked them to fill six big stone jars with water. 'Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast.' The master tasted it and was amazed: 'You have kept the best wine until now!' This was the first of Jesus' signs, and his disciples believed in him.
text.10-12: John calls the miracles of Jesus 'signs': they point to who he is. At Cana, Jesus blesses a wedding, and shows that he brings abundance: six jars of about twenty gallons each, which is a huge amount of wine. Mary notices the need and brings it to Jesus; her only advice to us is 'Do whatever he tells you.' The servants' obedience, filling jars with water to the brim, is part of the miracle. The Church sees here a hint of the wedding of Christ and his Church and of the Eucharist, where Jesus gives us his blood under the form of wine. Marriage is a sacrament, and Jesus begins his public life at a wedding.

talk: What did Mary notice?
What happened because the servants obeyed?
What does “Do whatever he tells you” mean for us?

stories.title: The Sermon on the Mount

text.4-6: Jesus sat on a hillside, and many people came to listen. He said, 'God blesses those who are gentle. God blesses those who are kind and who make peace. God blesses people with a pure heart.' Jesus said, 'You are the light of the world. Let your light shine!' Jesus tells us how to be truly happy.
text.7-9: A big crowd followed Jesus, so he went up on a mountainside, sat down and began to teach. He gave the Beatitudes, which tell us who is truly blessed: the poor in spirit, those who are sad, the gentle, those who hunger and thirst for what is right, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those who are treated badly for doing good. Jesus then said, 'You are the salt of the earth. You are the light of the world. No one lights a lamp and hides it under a basket. Let your light shine before others, so that they see the good you do and give glory to your Father in heaven.'
text.10-12: The Sermon on the Mount is Jesus' great teaching on how to live. He climbs a mountain, as Moses did, but instead of commandments he starts with blessings. 'Blessed' means happy in the deepest way, the happiness that comes from God and not from comfort or power. The eight Beatitudes describe the life of the saints: poor in spirit, gentle, merciful, pure in heart, peacemakers. They turn the world's ideas upside down. Jesus then calls us salt and light: we are not asked to be impressive, but to be visible and useful. The Catechism calls the Beatitudes 'the heart of Jesus' preaching'.

talk: Which Beatitude is your favourite?
How can you be a light at school or home?
Which saint was merciful, or a peacemaker?

stories.title: Jesus Teaches Us to Pray

text.4-6: The friends of Jesus said, 'Teach us to pray.' Jesus said, 'Pray like this: Our Father in heaven, may your name be holy. Give us this day our daily bread. Forgive us, as we forgive others.' We still say this prayer today, the Our Father. We can pray to God as our loving Father.
text.7-9: Jesus often went off by himself to pray. One day his disciples asked, 'Lord, teach us to pray.' Jesus said, 'When you pray, do not babble on to be heard, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him. Pray like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done on earth as in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins as we forgive those who sin against us. Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.' Jesus also said, 'If you forgive others, your Father will forgive you.'
text.10-12: The Our Father is the prayer Jesus himself gave. It is short, and holds everything: praise (hallowed be your name), the longing for God's kingdom, the need for daily bread, forgiveness given and received, and protection from evil. Jesus invites us to call God 'Abba', 'Father', a word of closeness. The first petitions are about God, and only then do we ask for ourselves. Notice it is 'Our' Father, a prayer for the whole family of God, not just 'my' needs. The Catechism calls it 'the summary of the whole Gospel', and we pray it at every Mass before Communion.

talk: What do we ask for in the Our Father?
Why is forgiveness part of the prayer?
When could you pray it slowly, a line at a time?

stories.title: The Friends Who Lowered the Roof

text.4-6: A man could not walk. His four friends wanted Jesus to heal him. The house was too full to get in. So they went up on the roof and dug a hole! They lowered their friend down on his mat, right in front of Jesus. Jesus saw how much they believed. He said, 'Your sins are forgiven. Stand up and walk!' The man stood up and walked home.
text.7-9: Jesus was teaching in a house in Capernaum, and the house was so crowded that no one else could get in, even at the door. Four men were carrying their paralysed friend on a mat. They could not get through the crowd, so they climbed up on the flat roof, made a hole, and lowered him down in front of Jesus. When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the man, 'Son, your sins are forgiven.' Some teachers of the law were upset: 'Only God can forgive sins!' Jesus said, 'So that you may know that I have authority on earth to forgive sins,' and he told the man, 'Get up, take your mat and go home.' The man got up at once and walked out. Everyone was amazed.
text.10-12: Four friends refuse to let a crowd keep them from Jesus, and Jesus responds to *their* faith. Before healing the body, he forgives the man's sins: this shows what he thinks matters most. His claim to forgive sins is a claim to be God, and the critics rightly notice that, but they do not believe him. The healing is the sign that he really has the authority. This story is a reminder of the power of praying for others and bringing others to Jesus. It is also the Gospel behind the sacrament of Confession: through his priests Jesus still says, 'Your sins are forgiven.'

talk: What did the friends do for the man?
Why did Jesus forgive his sins first?
Who could you bring to Jesus by praying for them?

stories.title: Jesus Calms the Storm

text.4-6: Jesus and his friends crossed the lake in a boat. Jesus was tired, and fell asleep. Then a big storm came! The waves splashed into the boat, and the friends were scared. 'Jesus, wake up!' Jesus stood up and said, 'Quiet! Be still!' The wind stopped, and the sea was calm. Jesus said, 'Why were you afraid?'
text.7-9: One evening Jesus said to his disciples, 'Let us go across to the other side of the lake.' They set off in a boat, and Jesus fell asleep on a cushion in the back. A fierce storm blew up, and the waves broke over the boat so that it was nearly full of water. The disciples woke Jesus: 'Teacher, do you not care that we are going to drown?' Jesus got up and said to the wind and sea, 'Peace! Be still!' The wind dropped and there was a great calm. He asked them, 'Why are you so afraid? Do you still have no faith?' They were amazed and asked each other, 'Who is this? Even the wind and sea obey him!'
text.10-12: The disciples include experienced fishermen, and they are terrified, so this was a real storm. The surprising detail is that Jesus is asleep in the boat: he is completely at peace in the Father's hands. When he wakes, he speaks to the storm as God spoke at creation, and the Psalms say that it is God who calms the roaring of the seas. The disciples' question, 'Who is this?', is the question of the whole Gospel. The Church has always seen the boat as an image of the Church, sometimes tossed about, but never abandoned: Jesus is in the boat.

talk: What are you afraid of when storms come?
What did the disciples learn about Jesus?
How can we ask Jesus for help when we are scared?

stories.title: Jesus Feeds the Crowd

text.4-6: A huge crowd followed Jesus, and they were hungry. A little boy had five loaves of bread and two fish. He shared them with Jesus. Jesus thanked God and broke the bread. And the food kept going and going! Everyone ate until they were full, and there were twelve baskets left over. Sharing is good, and God gives more than enough.
text.7-9: More than five thousand people had followed Jesus up the hill, and it was getting late. Jesus asked Philip, 'Where can we buy bread for these people to eat?' Philip said, 'Even eight months' wages would not buy enough!' Then Andrew said, 'There is a boy here with five barley loaves and two small fish, but what is that among so many?' Jesus told everyone to sit down on the grass. He took the loaves, gave thanks, and handed them out, and did the same with the fish. Everyone ate as much as they wanted. Afterwards Jesus said, 'Gather up the leftovers so nothing is wasted.' They filled twelve baskets.
text.10-12: This is the only miracle told in all four Gospels. The disciples count what they lack; a boy offers what little he has; Jesus makes it enough. Look at the verbs: Jesus 'took, gave thanks, broke and gave', the same four actions as at the Last Supper and at every Mass. John tells us it was near Passover, and the next day Jesus preaches the Bread of Life discourse: 'I am the bread of life; whoever eats this bread will live for ever.' God will take our small offerings and multiply them. Twelve baskets, one for each apostle, hint that the Church will go on feeding the world.

talk: What did the boy give?
What does Jesus do with the bread? Does it remind you of the Mass?
What small thing can you share this week?

stories.title: Jesus Walks on Water

text.4-6: The friends of Jesus were in a boat at night, and the wind blew hard. Then they saw Jesus walking on the water! 'Do not be afraid. It is me.' Peter said, 'Lord, let me come to you!' Peter stepped out and walked on the water. But when he looked at the big waves, he got scared and began to sink. Jesus took his hand: 'Why did you doubt?'
text.7-9: After feeding the crowd, Jesus sent his disciples ahead in the boat while he went up the mountain to pray. In the night the boat was far from land and struggling against the wind. Just before dawn Jesus came toward them, walking on the lake. They cried out in fear: 'It is a ghost!' But Jesus said, 'Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.' Peter called, 'Lord, if it is you, tell me to come to you on the water.' 'Come,' said Jesus. Peter stepped out of the boat and began walking toward Jesus, but when he noticed the strong wind, he became frightened and began to sink. 'Lord, save me!' Jesus reached out and caught him. 'You of little faith, why did you doubt?' When they climbed into the boat, the wind stopped, and they worshipped him.
text.10-12: Peter is the only one brave enough to ask to join Jesus on the waves, and for a short time he does the impossible, as long as his eyes are on Jesus. When he looks at the storm, he sinks. His prayer, 'Lord, save me!', is one of the shortest and best prayers in the Bible, and Jesus answers at once. The phrase 'It is I' can also be translated 'I AM', the name of God. The story shows Peter's impulsiveness, his faith and his weakness, which is why Jesus chooses him to lead. In the same way the Church, like the boat, is guided through storms by Peter's successors.

talk: What made Peter sink?
How can we keep our eyes on Jesus?
What is a short prayer you can say when you are afraid?

stories.title: The Good Samaritan

text.4-6: A man was hurt on a lonely road. A priest walked by. Another man walked by. Neither stopped. Then a man from Samaria came. He felt sorry for the hurt man. He cleaned his cuts, lifted him on his donkey and took him to an inn. He paid the innkeeper to take care of him. Jesus said, 'Go and do the same.'
text.7-9: A lawyer asked Jesus, 'Who is my neighbour?' Jesus told a story. A man travelling from Jerusalem to Jericho was attacked by robbers, beaten and left half-dead. A priest saw him and crossed the road to the other side. A Levite, who worked in the Temple, did the same. Then a Samaritan, a person from a group the Jews did not like, saw the man and felt pity. He bandaged his wounds with oil and wine, put him on his own donkey, took him to an inn and cared for him. The next day he paid the innkeeper and said, 'Look after him, and I will pay whatever else it costs.' Jesus asked, 'Which of the three was a neighbour?' The lawyer said, 'The one who showed mercy.' Jesus said, 'Go and do likewise.'
text.10-12: To answer the question 'Who is my neighbour?' Jesus tells a story that turns the question around: the real question is, 'Am I a neighbour?' The hero is a Samaritan, someone the audience would have thought of as an enemy, while the religious figures walk past. Mercy is not about who is like us; it is about seeing a need and acting. The Fathers of the Church saw in the story a picture of Christ himself, who stoops to the wounded human race, heals us with oil and wine (the sacraments) and brings us to the inn of the Church. The Catechism uses this parable when it teaches about love of neighbour.

talk: Why do you think the priest and Levite walked by?
Who are the “Samaritans” around you?
What could you do to show mercy this week?

stories.title: The Lost Sheep and the Lost Coin

text.4-6: A shepherd had one hundred sheep. One got lost! The shepherd left the ninety-nine and went to look for it. He looked and looked. When he found it, he put it on his shoulders and went home happy. 'Come and celebrate with me!' Jesus said, 'God is so happy when one person comes home to him.'
text.7-9: Some people grumbled that Jesus welcomed sinners and ate with them. So Jesus told them a story. 'Suppose one of you has a hundred sheep and loses one. Does he not leave the ninety-nine in the open country and look for the lost one until he finds it? When he finds it, he joyfully puts it on his shoulders and goes home. He calls his friends and neighbours: Rejoice with me, I have found my lost sheep!' Jesus also told about a woman who lost one of her ten silver coins, lit a lamp, swept the house and searched until she found it. 'In the same way,' said Jesus, 'there is more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine good people who do not need to repent.'
text.10-12: Two short parables, one message: God goes looking. The shepherd leaves the ninety-nine, which seems risky, and carries the sheep home on his shoulders: he does not scold it or make it walk. The woman sweeps the whole house for one coin. Both call their friends to celebrate. Jesus tells these stories to answer those who thought he was too welcoming; he says that heaven rejoices over every sinner who returns. Jesus is the Good Shepherd, and the cross is the place where he carried us home. When we go to Confession, we are the lost sheep being found.

talk: How does the shepherd feel when he finds his sheep?
Have you ever been lost, and then found?
How does God celebrate when we say sorry?

stories.title: The Sower and the Seeds

text.4-6: Jesus told a story about a farmer. He threw seeds on the ground. Some fell on the path, and the birds ate them. Some fell on stones, and they dried up. Some fell in thorns, and they were crowded out. But some fell on good soil, and they grew and grew! Jesus said, 'Listen to God’s word and let it grow in you.'
text.7-9: Jesus told a crowd about a sower who went out to plant seeds. Some seeds fell on the path, and birds came and ate them. Some fell on rocky ground, where the soil was thin, so the plants sprang up quickly but withered in the sun. Some fell among thorns that choked them. But some fell on good soil and produced a big harvest: thirty, sixty or even a hundred times what was planted. Later Jesus explained that the seed is God’s word, and the different soils are the different ways people hear it.
text.10-12: Jesus calls this the key to all his parables (Mark 4:13). The sower is generous, throwing seed everywhere, even where it may not grow, just as God offers his word to everyone. The soils are four ways of listening: hard, shallow, crowded and open. The point is not to judge other people but to look at our own hearts: what keeps the word from taking root in me? The harvest is surprising, far more than any farmer could expect, because the power is in the seed, which is God’s word.

talk: Which kind of soil do you think you are on most days?
What are the “thorns” that crowd out God’s word?
How can we make our hearts good soil?

stories.title: The Tiny Mustard Seed
