text.4-6: Jesus said, 'God’s kingdom is like a tiny mustard seed.' It is one of the smallest seeds. But when it is planted, it grows into a big tree. Birds come and make nests in its branches. Jesus also said it is like a little bit of yeast that makes a whole loaf of bread rise. Small things can grow into big things with God.
text.7-9: Jesus told two short stories about the kingdom of heaven. In the first, a man plants a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds. When it grows, it is bigger than the garden plants, and birds come and make nests in its branches. In the second, a woman mixes a little yeast into a large amount of flour, and in the end the whole lump of dough rises. Jesus was telling his friends that God’s kingdom may start very small, in a few people and ordinary acts of love, but it grows and grows, and no one can stop it.
text.10-12: The disciples were a small group of ordinary people, and the kingdom began with them. Jesus uses images of hidden growth: a seed under the soil, yeast in the dough. The kingdom is not a show of force; it works from within. The mustard tree welcoming birds recalls the prophets’ vision of all nations finding shelter in God’s kingdom (Ezekiel 17:23; Daniel 4:12). Catholics see in this the growth of the Church from a few apostles to every nation. It also invites patience in our own growth.

talk: What small thing grew into something big in your life?
Why does Jesus say the kingdom is like yeast?
What small act of love can you do this week?

stories.title: The Loving Father and His Two Sons

text.4-6: A son said to his father, 'Give me my share of the money.' He went far away and spent it all. Soon he was hungry. He thought, 'I will go home and say sorry.' While he was still far away, his father saw him and ran to hug him! 'My son was lost, and now he is found!' The father had a big party. God is like that father.
text.7-9: A man had two sons. The younger said, 'Father, give me my share of the property now.' He travelled to a distant country and wasted it all. When a famine came, he found work feeding pigs, and was so hungry he wanted to eat the pigs' food. 'I will go home,' he thought. 'I will say, Father, I have sinned. Treat me as one of your servants.' But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him, ran to him, hugged and kissed him. He called for the best robe, a ring and sandals, and a feast. The older brother was angry and would not come in. The father went out to him too: 'My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate: your brother was dead and is alive; he was lost and is found.'
text.10-12: This is the most famous of Jesus' stories, and it is about the Father's heart. The younger son asks for his inheritance, as if his father were dead, and the father lets him go. Notice what the father does when the son returns: he runs, which was undignified for an older man in that culture, interrupting the son's speech with a kiss. The son is restored with robe, ring and feast. But the story does not end there: the older brother, who stayed and worked, cannot stand the mercy. The father goes out to him as well. Both brothers need to learn the Father's love. Pope Francis and many saints return to this parable: it is the story of Confession.

talk: How did the father act when his son came home?
Which brother do you feel more like, the younger or the older?
What do you do when someone says sorry to you?

stories.title: Zacchaeus Climbs a Tree

text.4-6: Zacchaeus was a small man. He wanted to see Jesus, but the crowd was too tall. So he climbed a tree! Jesus looked up and said, 'Zacchaeus, come down! I am coming to your house today.' Zacchaeus was so happy. He said, 'I will give back what I took, and give to the poor.' Jesus loves to come to our house.
text.7-9: Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector in Jericho, and he was rich, because tax collectors often cheated people. Nobody liked him. He wanted to see who Jesus was, but he was short and the crowd was thick. So he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore-fig tree. When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said, 'Zacchaeus, hurry and come down. I must stay at your house today.' Zacchaeus hurried down and welcomed him gladly. The people muttered, 'He has gone to be the guest of a sinner.' But Zacchaeus stood up and said, 'Look, Lord, I will give half of what I own to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone I will pay back four times as much.' Jesus said, 'Today salvation has come to this house. The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.'
text.10-12: Zacchaeus is curious, not yet a believer. Jesus does what no one else does: he calls the man by name, invites himself over, and treats the despised sinner as a friend. The mercy comes first, and the change follows: Zacchaeus on his own promises half his wealth to the poor and fourfold repayment, which is much more than the law required. This is the shape of true conversion: love received, then love given back. The story is often read on the feast of the Dedication of a church, because Jesus comes to dwell in a house.

talk: Why did Zacchaeus climb the tree?
What did he do after meeting Jesus?
How can we welcome Jesus into our homes?

stories.title: Bartimaeus Can See

text.4-6: Bartimaeus could not see. He sat by the road and asked for help. When he heard that Jesus was coming, he shouted, 'Jesus, have mercy on me!' People told him to be quiet, but he shouted louder. Jesus stopped. 'What do you want me to do?' 'I want to see,' said Bartimaeus. Jesus healed him, and he followed Jesus.
text.7-9: Bartimaeus was a blind man who sat begging by the road outside Jericho. When he heard that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by, he shouted, 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!' Many people told him to be quiet, but he cried out even louder. Jesus stopped and said, 'Call him.' They said, 'Cheer up! He is calling you.' Bartimaeus threw off his cloak, jumped up and went to Jesus. Jesus asked, 'What do you want me to do for you?' 'Teacher, let me see again.' Jesus said, 'Go, your faith has healed you.' At once Bartimaeus could see, and he followed Jesus along the road.
text.10-12: Mark places this healing just before Jesus enters Jerusalem for his Passion. Bartimaeus ‘sees’ who Jesus is, calling him Son of David, before he receives his sight. The crowd tries to silence him, but persistence wins. He throws off his cloak, his one possession, and goes to Jesus. After he is healed, he follows Jesus ‘on the way’, which for Mark means the way to the Cross. The Church has used this story to teach about the prayer ‘Lord, have mercy’, which echoes his cry in the Mass.

talk: Why did Bartimaeus keep shouting?
What do you want Jesus to do for you?
What did Bartimaeus do after he could see?

stories.title: Martha and Mary

text.4-6: Jesus visited two sisters, Martha and Mary. Martha was busy cooking and cleaning. Mary sat at Jesus’ feet to listen. Martha said, 'Tell Mary to help me!' Jesus said, 'Martha, you are worried about many things. Mary has chosen what is best.' Jesus wants us to take time to listen to him.
text.7-9: Jesus came to the village where Martha and her sister Mary lived. Martha welcomed him and was busy with all the work of serving. Mary sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to what he said. Martha came to Jesus and said, 'Lord, don’t you care that my sister has left me to do the work alone? Tell her to help me!' Jesus answered gently, 'Martha, Martha, you are worried and upset about many things. Only one thing is needed. Mary has chosen what is better, and it will not be taken away from her.'
text.10-12: This short story is often read as a contrast between action and prayer, but Jesus does not scold Martha for serving. He names her worry. Hospitality is good; it becomes a burden when it crowds out the one thing needed, listening to him. The Church has long seen in the sisters two parts of every Christian life: service and contemplation, which belong together. Jesus says his word and presence come first. We serve better when we have first listened.

talk: What was Martha worried about?
How can you make time to listen to Jesus?
Is it better to serve or to pray? Why do we need both?

stories.title: The One Who Said Thank You

text.4-6: Ten men were very sick. They called out, 'Jesus, help us!' Jesus said, 'Go and show yourselves to the priests.' On the way, all ten were healed! But only one came back. He fell at Jesus’ feet and said, 'Thank you!' Jesus said, 'Where are the other nine?' It is good to say thank you to God.
text.7-9: As Jesus traveled to Jerusalem, ten men with a serious skin disease stood at a distance and called out, 'Jesus, Master, have pity on us!' Jesus told them to show themselves to the priests. As they went, they were healed. One of them, a Samaritan, came back praising God in a loud voice. He fell at Jesus’ feet and thanked him. Jesus asked, 'Were not all ten healed? Where are the other nine? Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?' Then he said, 'Get up and go. Your faith has made you well.'
text.10-12: All ten were healed as they obeyed Jesus’ word, but only one turned back to give thanks. He is the one who is least expected, a Samaritan. Jesus points out that gratitude is a mark of faith. The Greek word for ‘give thanks’ here is eucharistein, from which we get ‘Eucharist’. The Mass is the Church’s great thanksgiving. The story invites us to notice how many gifts we receive and to turn back to the Giver.

talk: Why did only one man come back?
Who can you thank today, and how?
What does the word “Eucharist” mean?

stories.title: The Widow’s Two Coins

text.4-6: Jesus sat in the Temple and watched people give money. Rich people gave a lot. Then a poor woman came. She put in two tiny coins. Jesus said, 'This woman gave more than anyone. She gave everything she had.' God cares about how much love we put into our gifts.
text.7-9: One day in the Temple, Jesus sat down opposite the place where people put their offerings. He watched the crowd putting in money. Many rich people put in large amounts. Then a poor widow came and dropped in two small copper coins, worth only a few cents. Jesus called his disciples over. 'I tell you the truth,' he said, 'this poor widow has put in more than all the others. They gave out of their wealth, but she, out of her poverty, put in everything she had to live on.'
text.10-12: Jesus values gifts not by size but by sacrifice and love. The rich give from their surplus; the widow gives from her need, trusting God to provide. Mark places this scene just before Jesus predicts the destruction of the Temple and speaks of his own gift of himself. The widow’s total self-giving foreshadows what Jesus is about to do on the Cross. The Church has seen in her a model of generosity and of trust in God’s care.

talk: Why did Jesus say the widow gave the most?
What can you give that costs you something?
How is the widow like Jesus?

stories.title: Jesus Blesses the Children

text.4-6: Parents brought their children to Jesus. His friends said, 'Go away! Jesus is busy.' But Jesus said, 'Let the children come to me! Do not stop them.' He hugged the children and blessed them. Jesus said, 'The kingdom of God belongs to people who are like children.' Jesus loves children very much.
text.7-9: People were bringing little children to Jesus so he could touch and bless them, but the disciples told them to stop. When Jesus saw this, he was indignant, which means very displeased. He said to the disciples, 'Let the little children come to me, and do not stop them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will never enter it.' Then he took the children in his arms, laid his hands on them and blessed them.
text.10-12: The disciples think children are a distraction; Jesus thinks they are the model. He does not say that children are perfect, but they know they need help, and they trust easily. Receiving the kingdom 'like a child' means receiving it as a gift, not something we earn. Jesus is not too busy for the smallest person. The Church takes this seriously: the early Church baptised whole families, including children, and today the Church begins the sacraments of initiation with children, trusting that God's grace is not limited by age.

talk: Why did the disciples send the children away?
What are children like that Jesus wants us to copy?
How does Jesus bless you?

stories.title: Jesus Raises Lazarus

text.4-6: Lazarus was Jesus' friend. He got very sick and died. His sisters Mary and Martha were sad, and Jesus cried too. Jesus went to the tomb and said, 'Lazarus, come out!' And Lazarus walked out, alive! Jesus is stronger than death. He gives life to everyone who believes in him.
text.7-9: Jesus had good friends in Bethany: Martha, Mary and their brother Lazarus. When Lazarus became ill, the sisters sent word to Jesus, but he did not come right away. By the time he arrived, Lazarus had been dead four days. Martha said, 'Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.' Jesus said to her, 'I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even though he dies, will live. Do you believe this?' 'Yes, Lord,' said Martha. When Jesus saw Mary weeping, he too wept. At the tomb he said, 'Take away the stone.' He prayed to his Father, then called out, 'Lazarus, come out!' The dead man came out, still wrapped in grave cloths. Jesus said, 'Unbind him and let him go.'
text.10-12: This is the last and greatest of Jesus' signs before Holy Week, and it has the shortest verse in the Bible: 'Jesus wept.' He knows the pain of loss and enters it. He also declares who he is: 'I am the resurrection and the life.' Martha's honest faith (she believes in the resurrection at the last day, but now Jesus asks her to believe in him) leads to one of the clearest professions of faith in John. Lazarus will die again, so this is a sign, not the final victory. Jesus will rise and not die again. This miracle makes the leaders determined to arrest Jesus. We read about it in Lent, before Easter.

talk: Why did Jesus cry?
What did Jesus tell Martha about himself?
How does this story give us hope when someone we love dies?

stories.title: Jesus Rides into Jerusalem

text.4-6: Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a little donkey. The people were so happy! They put their coats on the road. They waved palm branches and shouted, 'Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!' Jesus is our King, a gentle King. We remember this on Palm Sunday.
text.7-9: When Jesus and his disciples got near Jerusalem, he sent two of them ahead: 'Go to the village, and you will find a donkey tied there with her colt. Untie them and bring them to me.' This happened to fulfil what the prophet Zechariah said: 'Your king comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey.' The disciples put their cloaks on the donkey and Jesus sat on it. A large crowd spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and spread them. Crowds went before him and behind him, shouting, 'Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!' The whole city was stirred up, asking, 'Who is this?'
text.10-12: Jesus enters Jerusalem not on a warhorse but on a donkey, as the prophet Zechariah foretold: a king of peace. The crowds greet him with the words of Psalm 118, 'Hosanna', which means 'save us!', and wave palms, signs of victory. We do the same on Palm Sunday, when we carry palms in procession and read the long Passion account at Mass. Within days some of the same crowd will cry, 'Crucify him!' It reminds us that our own praise can be fickle. At every Mass, just before the Eucharistic prayer, we sing, 'Holy, holy, holy... Hosanna in the highest. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.'

talk: Why did Jesus ride a donkey instead of a horse?
What does Hosanna mean?
How do we welcome Jesus at Mass?

stories.title: The Last Supper

text.4-6: On the night before he died, Jesus had supper with his friends. He took bread, thanked God, broke it and said, 'This is my body.' He took a cup of wine and said, 'This is my blood.' He washed his friends' feet to show them how to serve. Jesus said, 'Do this to remember me.' We do this at Mass.
text.7-9: Before he died, Jesus shared the Passover meal with his twelve apostles in an upstairs room. During the meal he got up, wrapped a towel around his waist and began to wash their feet, the job of a servant. Peter said, 'You will never wash my feet!' Jesus said, 'Unless I wash you, you have no part with me.' Afterwards, Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it and gave it to them: 'This is my body, given for you. Do this in memory of me.' Then he took the cup: 'This cup is the new covenant in my blood, poured out for you.' He also gave them a new commandment: 'Love one another as I have loved you.'
text.10-12: This is the night when Jesus gave us the Eucharist and the priesthood, and the model of servant love. In the Passover tradition the family eats the lamb and remembers the exodus; Jesus changes bread and wine into his Body and Blood, and tells the apostles to 'do this' in his memory. This is what Catholics do at every Mass: the Last Supper, the cross and the resurrection are made present for us. Before this, Jesus washes feet, the lowest job, and says, 'I have given you an example.' We remember both on Holy Thursday, and the mandatum, the washing of feet, is part of that Mass.

talk: Why did Jesus wash his friends’ feet?
What do the words of Jesus over the bread and wine mean?
How can we serve other people like Jesus?

stories.title: The Servants and the Gifts

text.4-6: A master went on a trip. He gave three servants some money to take care of. Two servants used it well, and it grew. One servant hid his money in the ground. When the master came back, he was happy with the first two. 'Well done!' he said. Jesus tells us to use the gifts God gave us.
text.7-9: Jesus told a story about a man who went away and left his servants in charge of his property. He gave one servant five talents, another two, and another one, each according to ability. The first two put the money to work and doubled it. The third, afraid, dug a hole and hid the money. When the master returned after a long time, he praised the first two: 'Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many.' The third servant said, 'I was afraid.' The master was not pleased that he had not even tried.
text.10-12: A talent in Jesus’ day was a large sum of money. The master’s trust is a picture of what God gives us: time, abilities, faith and love, according to our capacity. The servants who risk are rewarded with joy and more responsibility; the one who hides his talent does so out of fear, and he has a wrong picture of the master. The parable is not about money but about how we answer God’s trust. The Church has used it to teach about the use of our gifts for the good of others and for the Kingdom.

talk: What gift has God given you?
Why was the third servant afraid?
How can you use your gifts to help others?

stories.title: Jesus Dies for Us

text.4-6: After supper, Jesus went to a garden to pray. His friends fell asleep. Soldiers came and took Jesus away, though he had done nothing wrong. Jesus carried his heavy cross. He was nailed to it. Even then, he said, 'Father, forgive them.' Jesus died because he loves us so much. His friends laid him in a tomb.
text.7-9: After the Last Supper, Jesus took his friends to a garden called Gethsemane. He prayed, 'Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me; yet not my will, but yours be done.' He was very sad. Judas, one of the twelve, came with soldiers and betrayed him with a kiss. Jesus was arrested and put on trial, and Peter, afraid, said three times that he did not know him. Jesus was sentenced to die on a cross. Soldiers made him carry the cross through the streets. On a hill called Calvary, he was crucified between two thieves. Jesus said, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.' To the good thief who asked to be remembered, he said, 'Today you will be with me in paradise.' At the end he said, 'Father, into your hands I commit my spirit.' His friends took his body and laid it in a tomb.
text.10-12: The Passion is the heart of the Gospel, and Luke shows Jesus as the one who forgives to the end: he heals the servant's ear in the garden, looks at Peter after his denial, speaks to the women of Jerusalem, forgives his executioners and welcomes the repentant thief. His final words are a prayer. Jesus did not die as a victim of chance; he gave himself freely, out of love, 'for us and for our salvation'. We remember this each Good Friday, and in the Stations of the Cross. Every crucifix reminds us of how much God loves us. The story is not the end, however.

talk: What did Jesus say about those who hurt him?
Why did Jesus die?
How can we thank Jesus for his love?

stories.title: Jesus Rises from the Dead

text.4-6: Early on Sunday morning, Mary Magdalene went to the tomb. The stone was rolled away, and Jesus' body was gone! Mary cried. Then someone said, 'Mary.' It was Jesus! He was alive! 'Go and tell my friends,' he said. Mary ran to tell them, 'I have seen the Lord!' Jesus is alive! We sing Alleluia on Easter Sunday.
text.7-9: Very early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene went to the tomb and found the stone rolled away. She ran to Peter and John: 'They have taken the Lord out of the tomb!' The two ran to the tomb, and John, who got there first, waited for Peter. Peter went inside and saw the burial cloths lying there. John saw and believed. Mary stood outside the tomb, crying. Two angels asked, 'Woman, why are you weeping?' She turned and saw a man whom she thought was the gardener. Jesus said, 'Mary.' She knew his voice. 'Rabboni!' she cried. Jesus said, 'Go and tell my brothers I am ascending to my Father and your Father.' Mary went and told the disciples, 'I have seen the Lord!'
text.10-12: On Easter morning, John gives us the most intimate scene: Mary Magdalene, still weeping, does not recognise Jesus until he says her name. The Good Shepherd 'calls his own sheep by name'. She is the first witness of the Resurrection, so the Church has called her 'apostle to the apostles'. The empty tomb is not just a missing body: Jesus rises with a new, glorified body. His words, 'my Father and your Father', tell us that, through Jesus, we are God's children. Easter is the centre of the Christian year; every Sunday is a little Easter.

talk: Why did Mary not recognise Jesus at first?
What made her know him?
What does it mean to you that Jesus is alive?

stories.title: The Road to Emmaus

text.4-6: Two friends were walking sadly to a village called Emmaus. A stranger joined them. He explained the Bible to them. When they got home, the stranger broke bread and blessed it. Then they knew: it was Jesus! He vanished. They said, 'Did our hearts not burn when he spoke?' They ran back to tell everyone.
text.7-9: On the day Jesus rose, two followers were walking from Jerusalem to the village of Emmaus, talking sadly about everything that had happened. Jesus himself came up and walked with them, but they did not recognise him. 'What are you discussing?' he asked. They told him about Jesus, who had been crucified, and about the women who said the tomb was empty. Jesus explained how all the Scriptures pointed to the Messiah's suffering and glory. When they arrived, they begged him, 'Stay with us.' At table he took the bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them. Their eyes were opened, and they recognised him, and he disappeared. They said to each other, 'Were not our hearts burning while he spoke to us on the road?' They hurried back to Jerusalem to tell the others.
text.10-12: Luke tells us how to meet the risen Lord. First, he walks with us, even when we are sad and do not know it. Second, he opens the Scriptures: our hearts burn. Third, he is known 'in the breaking of the bread'. This is the pattern of the Mass: the Liturgy of the Word, then the Liturgy of the Eucharist, and then we are sent to tell others. 'Stay with us, Lord' has become a prayer, and Pope Saint John Paul II even wrote a letter, 'Stay with us, Lord', on the Eucharist, drawing on this story.

talk: Why did the two travellers not know Jesus?
When did they recognise him?
How is the Mass like this story?

stories.title: The Holy Spirit Comes

text.4-6: Jesus went up to heaven. His friends waited together and prayed. Then, on the day of Pentecost, a wind blew, and flames like little fires rested on each one of them. They were filled with the Holy Spirit! They were not afraid anymore. They told everyone about Jesus. People from many countries all understood them. The Church began!
text.7-9: After Jesus went up to heaven, he told his friends to wait in Jerusalem. About 120 followers, including Mary, were praying together on the day of Pentecost, fifty days after Passover. Suddenly there was a sound like a strong wind that filled the whole house. They saw tongues like flames come to rest on each of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages. A big crowd gathered, people from many different countries, and each heard them speaking in his own language. Peter stood and told them about Jesus. 'What should we do?' they asked. Peter said, 'Repent and be baptised.' About three thousand people were baptised that day.
text.10-12: Pentecost is the birthday of the Church. The disciples who had been hiding behind locked doors are transformed: Peter, who once denied Jesus, preaches boldly. Fire and wind are signs of God's power and presence, and the languages undo Babel: people of every nation hear the good news. Peter's first sermon is a pattern for evangelisation: he proclaims Jesus, calls for repentance and baptism, and the new community 'devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, to fellowship, to the breaking of the bread and to prayers'. In Confirmation, the Holy Spirit is given to us for the same mission.

talk: What signs showed the Holy Spirit had come?
How did the disciples change after Pentecost?
What gift of the Spirit would you ask for?

stories.title: Saul Meets Jesus

text.4-6: Saul did not like Christians, and he wanted to put them in prison. On the road to Damascus, a bright light shone, and he fell to the ground! A voice said, 'Saul, why are you hurting me?' It was Jesus! Saul could not see. A kind man named Ananias prayed for him, and he could see again. Saul became Paul, and told everyone about Jesus.
text.7-9: Saul was a strict Jewish leader who thought the followers of Jesus were wrong, and he went from town to town arresting them. On the road to Damascus, a light from heaven flashed around him, and he fell to the ground. A voice said, 'Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?' 'Who are you, Lord?' he asked. 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.' Saul got up, but was blind. For three days he did not eat or drink. In Damascus, God told a disciple named Ananias to go to Saul. Ananias was afraid, but he obeyed and laid his hands on Saul: 'Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.' Something like scales fell from Saul's eyes. He was baptised and began to preach that Jesus is the Son of God.
text.10-12: Paul's own story is the greatest example of how God's mercy can reach anyone. Saul is the Church's fiercest enemy, and Jesus calls him personally. The Lord's words, 'Why do you persecute me?', show that Jesus is so united with his followers that whatever is done to them is done to him: this is the Church as the Body of Christ. Ananias takes a risk to welcome the man who might kill him, and calls him 'brother'. Paul goes on to write many of the letters in the New Testament and to take the Gospel to Europe. The Church celebrates his conversion on 25 January.

talk: Why did Saul change?
How was Ananias brave?
Who could you pray for who seems far from God?

stories.title: Philip and the Traveler

text.4-6: An angel told Philip, 'Go to the desert road.' There he saw a man in a chariot, reading from the Bible. 'Do you understand what you are reading?' asked Philip. 'How can I, unless someone explains?' said the man. Philip told him about Jesus. The man asked to be baptized. They went down to some water, and Philip baptized him. The man went home full of joy.
text.7-9: An angel told Philip to go south on the road from Jerusalem to Gaza. There he met an Ethiopian official, the treasurer of the queen, riding in his chariot and reading aloud from the prophet Isaiah. The Spirit told Philip, 'Go and stay near that chariot.' Philip asked, 'Do you understand what you are reading?' The man said, 'How can I, unless someone explains it to me?' He invited Philip to sit with him. Beginning with the passage in Isaiah, Philip told him the good news about Jesus. When they came to some water, the man said, 'Look, here is water. What stops me from being baptized?' Philip baptized him. Then the Spirit took Philip away, and the official went on his way rejoicing.
text.10-12: This is one of the first stories of the Church reaching beyond Israel. The Ethiopian official is an outsider on many counts, but he is searching, reading Isaiah 53 about the suffering servant. Philip’s way of teaching is a model: he listens, asks a question, starts where the person is, and explains Scripture in light of Jesus. The result is Baptism, and joy. The Church has long used this passage to show that Scripture needs a guide, and that the Word leads to the sacraments.

talk: What was the man reading, and why did he need help?
How did Philip start the conversation?
Who has helped you understand the Bible or the faith?

stories.title: Singing in Prison

text.4-6: Paul and Silas were put in jail for telling people about Jesus. At midnight they were not sad. They prayed and sang songs to God! The other prisoners listened. Suddenly there was an earthquake, and the doors opened! The jailer was afraid, but Paul said, 'We are all here.' The jailer asked, 'How can I be saved?' He and his family became Christians.
text.7-9: In the city of Philippi, Paul and Silas were arrested, beaten and put into the inner cell of the prison with their feet fastened in stocks. About midnight, they were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening. Suddenly there was a violent earthquake. The prison doors flew open, and everyone’s chains came loose. The jailer woke up and, thinking the prisoners had escaped, was about to kill himself. But Paul shouted, 'Don’t harm yourself! We are all here!' The jailer asked, 'What must I do to be saved?' They said, 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you and your household will be saved.' He washed their wounds, and he and his whole family were baptized that night.
text.10-12: Paul and Silas are in pain and in the dark, yet they pray and sing. Their joy is not in their circumstances; it is in God. The earthquake does not make them run; they stay, and that act of care for the jailer opens the door to his faith. The jailer, who had put them in chains, ends up washing their wounds and feeding them, and the whole household is baptized. The story shows how the Gospel spreads through suffering endured with joy, and how conversion bears fruit in mercy.

talk: Why were Paul and Silas singing in prison?
Why did Paul tell the jailer not to hurt himself?
What happened to the jailer and his family?

stories.title: The New Heaven and Earth

text.4-6: At the end of the Bible, God shows a beautiful picture. There will be a new heaven and a new earth. God will live with his people. 'He will wipe away every tear. There will be no more sadness or pain or death.' God says, 'Look, I am making everything new!' This is what we hope for.
text.7-9: The last book of the Bible, Revelation, was written by John to give hope to Christians who were suffering. John saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away. He saw the holy city, a new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, like a bride dressed for her husband. A loud voice said, 'Look! God's dwelling is among his people. He will live with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them. He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or crying or pain.' The one on the throne said, 'See, I am making everything new!'
text.10-12: Revelation ends the Bible where Genesis began, in a garden city where God dwells with his people. The vision is full of symbols, and John does not give us a map of heaven; he gives us a promise: God himself will come to live with us, and every tear will be wiped away. The old order of death and pain is gone. We do not escape the world; it is renewed. Catholics profess this in the Creed: 'I look forward to the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come.' This hope is what makes it possible to keep going through suffering, and to love now.

talk: What do you think will be best about heaven?
Why does God wipe away tears himself?
How can we help make things new here and now?
